About: Series & Parallel — Why Adding a Resistor Can Lower Resistance

Source

Topic
Current electricity — combinations of resistors (NCERT Class 12, Ch. 3)
Simulation
Same two resistors wired two ways, side by side, with charge-flow density tied to current.
Concept
Adding a resistor in parallel LOWERS the total resistance — because you have opened a second path, not added an obstacle.
Serves
Series adds; parallel is reciprocal and below the smaller branch; the smaller resistance carries the larger current.
Inquiry
Predict what a 20 Ω in parallel with a 10 Ω does to the total: rise to 30 Ω, fall below 10 Ω, or stay at 10 Ω.

“More resistors means more resistance.” True in series; wrong in parallel.

Guided Inquiry

Series first — the resistances add

R₁ = 10 Ω and R₂ = 20 Ω are wired in series. Every charge passes through both, so the two obstacles add: Rseries = R₁ + R₂ = 30 Ω. One current, the same everywhere; the supply voltage divides between them, V₁ + V₂.

Predict — 20 Ω added in parallel with 10 Ω

You have a 10 Ω resistor. You now connect a 20 Ω resistor in parallel with it. What does the total resistance become?

Which branch carries more?

A 3 A supply feeds that same 10 Ω and 20 Ω in parallel. Which branch carries the larger current?

Both predictions settled

At 10 Ω and 20 Ω the parallel total reads 6.67 Ω — below both branches — and the flow splits: 2 A through the 10 Ω, 1 A through the 20 Ω. Both branches sit at the same 20 V, which is why the smaller resistance takes the larger current.

Series and parallel are opposites: series shares the current and divides the voltage; parallel shares the voltage and divides the current. You did not add an obstacle — you opened a second path.

Play freely

All three sliders are live. Try equal resistances (both 10 Ω): series 20 Ω, parallel 5 Ω — exactly half. Try 10 Ω with 90 Ω: parallel is 9 Ω, barely below 10 Ω, because a large branch barely helps. In every case Rparallel is below the smaller branch — never a hardcoded number, always the engine's answer.

Series & Parallel

✦Learn this with the AI tutor

01

At a glance

Two resistors can share a circuit in two ways, one after the other or side by side. The sim wires the same two resistors both ways at once and feeds each wiring the same total current. You can then compare the total resistance of each, and the current in each resistor.

What you'll learn

  • How the total resistance of two resistors depends on how they are wired.
  • Which quantity, current or voltage, the resistors share in each wiring, and which one they divide.
  • How a supply current divides between two branches, and how to calculate each share.
The same two resistors wired one after the other on the left, and side by side on the right.

What's on screen

  • R₁ (amber zig-zag): the first resistor, in both circuits.
  • R₂ (blue zig-zag): the second resistor, in both circuits.
  • Charges (dots): they stream round each loop. The denser the dots, the larger the current.
  • Series panel (left) and Parallel panel (right): each shows its battery, with the supply voltage it needs, and its total resistance underneath.
  • Equivalent resistance panel (sidebar): both totals, and a check against the smaller branch.
See itPress Play with R₁ = 10 Ω, R₂ = 20 Ω and I = 3.0 A. Watch for: charges streaming round both circuits, and the amber and blue resistor labels in each panel.

03

In series the resistances add

In series there is a single path, so every charge passes through both resistors and the same current I flows in each. The supply voltage divides between them: V = V₁ + V₂ = IR₁ + IR₂ = I(R₁ + R₂). The pair therefore acts as one resistor:

Rseries = R₁ + R₂
Same current through both, and the voltage divides in proportion to R.

With R₁ = 10 Ω, R₂ = 20 Ω and I = 3.0 A, Rseries = 30 Ω. The voltages are V₁ = 3.0 × 10 = 30 V and V₂ = 3.0 × 20 = 60 V, so the battery must supply 90 V. The total is larger than either resistor, because every charge has to get past both. The bigger resistor takes the bigger share of the voltage.

See itPlay the defaults and read the series panel. Watch for: Rseries = 30.00 Ω in the sidebar, and V₁ = 30.0 V + V₂ = 60.0 V = 90.0 V in the panel.
04

In parallel the reciprocals add

In parallel both resistors connect to the same two points, so each has the full voltage V across it. Each takes its own current, I₁ = V/R₁ and I₂ = V/R₂, and the supply delivers the sum I = I₁ + I₂ = V(1/R₁ + 1/R₂). Writing V = IRparallel gives:

1/Rparallel = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂
Same voltage across both, and the current divides.

For two resistors this is Rparallel = R₁R₂/(R₁ + R₂). With 10 Ω and 20 Ω, 1/R = 1/10 + 1/20 = 3/20, so Rparallel = 20/3 = 6.67 Ω. That is below both resistors. A second resistor in parallel opens a second path for the charge, so the total opposition falls. At 3.0 A the supply needs only 3.0 × 6.67 = 20 V, against 90 V for the series circuit.

See itPlay the defaults and read the parallel panel and the sidebar. Watch for: Rparallel = 6.67 Ω, shown with yes ✓ next to the smaller-branch check.
05

The smaller resistance carries the larger current

Both parallel branches sit at the same voltage, and I = V/R, so the branch currents are in inverse proportion to the resistances: I₁/I₂ = R₂/R₁. Written out for a total current I, this is the current divider:

I₁ = I·R₂/(R₁ + R₂),   I₂ = I·R₁/(R₁ + R₂)
Each branch carries the share set by the other resistor.

At I = 3.0 A, the 10 Ω branch carries I₁ = 3 × 20/30 = 2.0 A and the 20 Ω branch carries I₂ = 3 × 10/30 = 1.0 A. They add to 3.0 A. Check the shared voltage: 2.0 × 10 = 20 V and 1.0 × 20 = 20 V. Series and parallel are opposites. Series shares the current and divides the voltage. Parallel shares the voltage and divides the current.

See itPlay the defaults and read the labels under the parallel branches. Watch for: I₁ = 2.00 A and I₂ = 1.00 A, and V₁ = V₂ = 20.0 V at the foot of the panel.
06

Parallel stays below the smaller resistor

Because Rparallel = R₁ · R₂/(R₁ + R₂) and the fraction R₂/(R₁ + R₂) is always less than 1, Rparallel is less than R₁. The same argument gives less than R₂. With R₁ = 10 Ω the partner changes the totals like this:

R₂RseriesRparallel
10 Ω20 Ω5.00 Ω
20 Ω30 Ω6.67 Ω
90 Ω100 Ω9.00 Ω
100 Ω110 Ω9.09 Ω

Two equal resistors in parallel give exactly half of one. A very large partner barely helps, since almost no current takes its branch, so Rparallel creeps toward 10 Ω without reaching it. Series behaves the other way: Rseries is always above the larger resistor.

See itKeep R₁ = 10 Ω and raise R₂ to 90 Ω. Watch for: Rparallel = 9.00 Ω, still under the 10 Ω smaller branch, while Rseries = 100.00 Ω.
07

Where it matters

  • Household wiring. Appliances are wired in parallel across the same supply voltage, so each draws its own current and switching one off does not affect the others. Plugging in one more appliance adds a branch, lowers the total resistance and raises the total current. That is why an overloaded socket trips its breaker.
  • Voltage divider. Two resistors in series divide a supply voltage in proportion to their resistances. Here V₂/V₁ = R₂/R₁ = 2.
  • Making a value. Two 10 Ω resistors give 20 Ω in series or 5 Ω in parallel. Series reaches larger values than the parts, and parallel reaches smaller ones.
  • A mirror of capacitors. The capacitor rules are these rules with series and parallel swapped.
08

Summary

In one line. How two resistors are wired sets their total resistance, and it also sets which quantity they share and which they divide.

Key points

  • Series: same I through both, Rseries = R₁ + R₂.
  • Parallel: same V across both, 1/Rparallel = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂.
  • In parallel, I₁/I₂ = R₂/R₁, so the smaller R carries more.

Common mix-ups

  • "More resistors always means more resistance." True in series. In parallel each extra resistor opens another path and the total falls.
  • "Parallel resistors carry equal currents." They share the voltage, not the current. The current divides in inverse proportion to R.
  • "The total in parallel can be anywhere." It is always below the smallest branch, and for two equal resistors it is half of one.

Things to try on your own

  • Find R₁ and R₂ that give Rseries = 50 Ω and Rparallel = 12 Ω, then check both readouts.
  • Set R₁ = R₂ and confirm that Rparallel is half of R₁.
  • Set R₁ = 10 Ω, R₂ = 40 Ω and I = 5.0 A. Work out I₁ and I₂ before you read the labels.
